Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: When did a computer first learn to understand human speech? Today we talk to phones and they answer back. How long did it take to get here? The answer is at the end of this email.

  • The European Commission confirms that a cyberattack on its computers was carried out with an AI tool. The European Commission, which runs the EU’s daily business, has confirmed that a cyberattack noticed on 22 October was “an AI generated cyber campaign” using a publicly available tool. To be safe it switched off several staff systems, including pay slips and medical refunds; most are back. The Commission has found no evidence of a wide theft of staff data and won’t say who was behind it. The press names the tool as ARTEX, a free program meant for testing defences, which the EU’s own cyber team warned about on 5 November; the Commission has not confirmed the name. Read more and the background.
  • Signal, the private messaging app, starts blocking AI assistants from reading chats off the phone’s screen. Signal, the messaging app known for privacy, says the AI assistants now built into phones are a new threat: they can read a conversation off the screen, where it is no longer protected. So on the newest iPhones Signal now blocks screenshots in the app, and on Android it turns on a protective setting when an AI assistant tries to read the screen. It admits the fix is incomplete, and it cannot block this on Mac computers at all. It is asking Apple, Google and Microsoft for a simple way for apps to keep AI out. Read more and the background.
  • OpenAI says it has made it far harder for others to copy its newest models by harvesting their “thinking”. Some companies build AI cheaply by questioning a rival’s model millions of times and training their own on the answers; this is called distillation. OpenAI says its newest model now resists attempts to pull out its hidden step-by-step reasoning far better: in its own tests, success fell from 54% to 0.2%. It also bans thousands of accounts a week. The figures are OpenAI’s own. The report mentions that Anthropic, which makes Claude, the AI writing this digest, has found something similar. Read more and the background.
  • Google’s Gemini can now work Mac programs by itself, while Apple is said to be building its own such assistant. Google’s Gemini app for Mac computers can now operate other programs by itself: you describe a chore, such as filling in forms from files in a folder, and it clicks and types in a separate window while you watch, approving important steps. It is starting in English in the US for paying users. Apple is reportedly building its own such assistant and has meanwhile made it harder for outside ones to take control of a Mac. The Decoder lists Anthropic, which makes Claude, the AI writing this digest, among companies that already offer such tools. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Four American senators propose that listed companies tell investors more about AI, as Anthropic’s arrival on the stock exchange draws attention in Washington, Google opens Genie 4, a program that invents a video world you can walk around in, to outside developers, A Google DeepMind researcher asks what comes after AI that matches people.

Answer to the question of the day. Earlier than most people think, but only a very little at first. The Russian magazine Sistemny Blok tells the story in five steps. In 1952 the American Bell Labs built a machine called Audrey that recognised spoken digits from zero to nine, and only from one voice, with a pause after each word. In the 1960s a program called ELIZA, written at MIT, answered typed messages by playing a psychotherapist: it simply turned the person’s words back into questions from a fixed script. Its author meant it to show how shallow such conversation is, yet people grew attached to it anyway. In 1978 a system called HARPY, at Carnegie Mellon University, knew over a thousand words and could follow whole sentences spoken without pauses. In 1995 a chat program called ALICE could keep track of the previous exchange and draw simple conclusions. And in 2011 Apple put Siri in a phone, joining voice commands to a chatting program; it learned to search the web, make calls and set reminders. The article’s point is that these machines gained skills slowly, one at a time, and that even Siri still makes people adapt to it, not the other way round; many such systems also work far better in English than in smaller languages. Its closing thought is that today’s large language models are speeding everything up. The article is from January 2025, so the newest assistants are not in it. Sistemny Blok, “The history of dialogue systems: from recognising digits to Siri” (January 2025) (article in Russian).
